'''''Aristolochia paucinervis''''' is a [[herbaceous]] plant in the family [[Aristolochiaceae]] endemic to the western [[Mediterranean Basin]].

==Description==
''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is a perennial [[geophyte]] plant. Its saxophone-shaped flowers are used to attract their pollinators (flies).<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Kew)|first1=Hassan Rankou (Royal Botanic Garden|last2=Taleb|first2=Mohammed Sghir|last3=University)|first3=Ahmed Ouhammou (Cady Ayyad|last4=Martin|first4=Gary|date=2014-01-16|title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Aristolochia paucinervis|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en|journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The genus name ''[[Aristolochia]]'' is comprised the ancient Greek words Aristos and Lochia which translate to "best" and "childbirth" respectively due to its historic uses in traditional medicine where the roots were used as a stimulant used during childbirth to promote labour.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Heinrich|first1=Michael|last2=Chan|first2=Jennifer|last3=Wanke|first3=Stefan|last4=Neinhuis|first4=Christoph|last5=Simmonds|first5=Monique S. J.|date=2009-08-17|title=Local uses of Aristolochia species and content of nephrotoxic aristolochic acid 1 and 2—A global assessment based on bibliographic sources|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874109003468|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|language=en|volume=125|issue=1|pages=108–144|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2009.05.028|pmid=19505558 |issn=0378-8741|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The authority of the species is Pomel, who first published the species in ''Nouveau Materiaux pour la Flore Atlantique'' 1874.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Aristolochia paucinervis Pomel {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:93208-1|access-date=2021-12-06|website=Plants of the World Online|language=en}}</ref> ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is also commonly referred to as 'Barraztam' in [[Morocco]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Gadhi|first1=C. A|last2=Weber|first2=M|last3=Mory|first3=F|last4=Benharref|first4=A|last5=Lion|first5=C|last6=Jana|first6=M|last7=Lozniewski|first7=A|date=1999-10-01|title=Antibacterial activity of Aristolochia paucinervis Pomel|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874198002128|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|language=en|volume=67|issue=1|pages=87–92|doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(98)00212-8|pmid=10616964 |issn=0378-8741|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Plant description ==
''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is a climbing [[Perennial plant|perennial]] vine plant that can grow up to heights of 0.5m in the [[understory]] of the forest.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Aristolochia paucinervis Pomel - Encyclopedia of Life|url=https://eol.org/pages/2867518|access-date=2021-12-06|website=eol.org}}</ref> The plant has simple, smooth, broad leaves 3-5cm wide with a triangular-oval blade shape and palmate veins.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Aristolochia paucinervis|url=https://www.tela-botanica.org/eflore/consultation/popup.php?referentiel=bdtfx&niveau=2&module=fiche&action=fiche&num_nom=6463&type_nom=nom_scientifique&nom=aristolochia|access-date=2021-12-06|website=www.tela-botanica.org}}</ref> This plant possesses a [[tuber]] which acts as storage for the plant.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Berjano|first1=Regina|last2=Vega|first2=Clara de|last3=Arista|first3=Montserrat|last4=Ortiz|first4=Pedro L.|last5=Talavera|first5=Salvador|date=2006|title=A Multi-Year Study of Factors Affecting Fruit Production in Aristolochia paucinervis (Aristolochiaceae)|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=93|issue=4|pages=599–606|doi=10.3732/ajb.93.4.599 |jstor=4125573 |pmid=21646221 |issn=0002-9122|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Flower description ==
[[File:Aristolochia paucinervis FlowersCloseup3 12April2009 DehesaBoyaldePuertollano.jpg|thumb|left|Flower close-up]]
The flowers have two different [[phenotype]]s: yellow-white flowers and brown-purple flowers.<ref name=":1" /> The flower is protogynous which means that the male reproductive organs and female reproductive organs develop at different times to prevent self-fertilization.<ref name=":1" /> The flowers has a tube shaped [[perianth]] derived from a modified calyx. The perianth forms a reproductive structure known as the gynostemium which houses the fused [[Style (botany)|styles]], [[Stigma (botany)|stigmata]] and [[anthers]].<ref name=":1" /> Flowers produce around  2100 pollen grains and 42 ovules.<ref name=":1" />

== Pollination mechanism ==
''Aristolochia paucinervis'' undergoes pollination by exuding a strong smell that attracts small [[Diptera]] (flies) into its tube shaped periant. The flies remain trapped as the hairs prevent them from escaping for a period of time. When the anthers mature, pollen is deposited onto the fly and the hairs inside the tube wither which allow the insect to escape and pollinate another flower.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Chiricahua Mtns 2014|url=https://www2.palomar.edu/users/warmstrong/Portal146.htm|access-date=2021-12-06|website=www2.palomar.edu}}</ref>

The pollination mechanism is said to be deceptive because the pollinators are [[Saprophagy|saprophagous]] which means that they feed on decaying matter and do not feed on the nectar or pollen that is provided by the plant.<ref name=":1" />

== Fruit ==
After flowering, the stigma and perianth wilt, exposing the ovary on the plant.<ref name=":1" /> The ovary then develops into a [[Capsule (fruit)|capsular]] fruit up to 3cm in length which contains around 11 large seeds.<ref name=":1" />

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Distribution_of_Plant.png|thumb|A map showing the native range of the plant]]
''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is widely distributed throughout the western [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]], including [[Madeira]] and the [[Canary Islands]] of [[Macaronesia]], [[Morocco]], the [[Iberian Peninsula]] (most of [[Portugal]] and primarily southern [[Spain]]), the [[Balearic Islands]], southern [[France]], a small part of [[Algeria]] and is thought to be extinct in [[Tunisia]].

It can be found at elevations between 500 - 2,500m.

It grows in sandy and stony pastures, meadows, rocky cliffs, scrub, woodlands clearings, cultivated fields, weed of crops, wood grassy mountains and Mediterranean forest and prefers moist humid to dry substrates, stony, clay and sandy soils, relatively poor with a basic pH.<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" /><ref name="flora-on">{{cite web |title=Aristolochia paucinervis Pomel |url=https://flora-on.pt/#/1Aristolochia+paucinervis |publisher=Flora-on |access-date=17 December 2020}}</ref>

== Traditional uses ==
Traditional uses of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' include its role in Moroccan medicine, where it is locally known as "Barraztam".<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title=Aristolochia paucinervis - Useful Temperate Plants|url=http://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Aristolochia+paucinervis|access-date=2021-12-06|website=temperate.theferns.info}}</ref> The powdered root or [[rhizome]] of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is mixed with salted [[smen]] - this mixture can be applied topically to treat skin infections, injuries and gas gangrene, or ingested with honey or salted butter to treat abdominal pain and upper respiratory tract infections.<ref name=":5" />

== Medicinal uses ==
''Aristolochia paucinervis'' has several medicinal uses. Ingesting the dried powdered root of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' is used as a treatment of aortic palpitations, [[constipation]], intestinal disorders, [[colic]], gas gangrene, and as a poison antidote for snakebites.<ref name=":6">{{cite book |last1=Lihong |first1=Liu |last2=Weiss |first2=Gabriel |last3=Buchtel |first3=Henry |last4=Wilms |first4=Sabine |editor-last=Fruehauf |editor-first=Heiner |chapter=Glossary of Herbs and Formulas |title=Classical Chinese Medicine |date=2019 |pages=625–628 |doi=10.2307/j.ctvzsmc00.18 |publisher=The Chinese University of Hong Kong Press|s2cid=243549649 }}</ref> Additionally, the [[methanol]] extract from the leaves of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' has anti-fungal properties and is effective against pathogenic fungi responsible for skin diseases and infections such as tinea, dermatitis, and mycoses.<ref name=":6" /> The most susceptible fungi were ''[[Epidermophyton floccosum]]'' and ''[[Trichophyton violaceum]]'' in contrast to ''[[Trichophyton mentagrophytes]]'' and ''[[Trichophyton rubrum]]'' which were less sensitive to the fractions tested.<ref name=":6" /> The leaves of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' possess antibacterial activity - in a study conducted by Gadhi et al., ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' exhibited activity against ''[[Clostridium perfringens]], [[Clostridioides difficile (bacteria)|Clostridioides difficile]], [[Enterococcus faecalis]], [[Micrococcus luteus]],'' and ''[[Bacillus subtilis]]'', as seen by the minimum inhibitory concentration.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gadhi|first1=C. A.|last2=Benharref|first2=A.|last3=Jana|first3=M.|last4=Basile|first4=A. M.|last5=Contet-Audonneau|first5=N.|last6=Fortier|first6=B.|date=2001|title=Antidermatophytic properties of extracts from the leaves ofAristolochia paucinervis Pomel|journal=Phytotherapy Research|volume=15|issue=1|pages=79–81|doi=10.1002/1099-1573(200102)15:1<79::aid-ptr953>3.0.co;2-k|pmid=11180530 |s2cid=43815136 |issn=0951-418X}}</ref> The whole plant of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' can be used externally to treat [[ringworm]] and wounds when dried and pulverized.<ref name=":6" /> Plants of the [[Aristolochiaceae]] family contain [[aristolochic acid]]s (AAs) - this compound has a long history of use in herbal medicine that dates back to the 5th century in China and even earlier in Europe.<ref name=":6" /> The presence of AA in the roots of the plant stimulates white blood cell activity and speeds wound healing. AAs are also used to treat [[tuberculosis]], [[hepatitis]], [[Liver Cirrhosis|liver cirrhosis]], and infantile pneumonia.<ref name=":4" />

== Anticancer compounds ==
In addition to its many medicinal uses, ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' exhibits anti-cancer properties. Research has suggested that ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' contains a peptide, EnnA, that directly inhibits [[Hsp90|HSP90]], a cell protector hijacked by cancer to avoid being attacked by the immune system. Thus, by inhibiting HSP90, EnnA allows the immune system to respond to cancer cells.<ref name=":3" /> Despite its cytotoxic effects against cancer cell lines and apoptosis-induced pathways, the preparation of ''Aristolochia paucinervis'' for cancer is banned in many countries.<ref name=":3" />

== Toxic compounds and toxicity ==
Although there are few reports of acute human or animal poisoning by the ''Aristolochia paucinervis'', plants of the [[Aristolochiaceae]] family are considered dangerous when consumed over long periods of time as the roots contain [[aristolochic acid]]s (AAs). AAs are responsible for renal damage due to their nephrotoxic effects. When taken internally, AAs can be carcinogenic -  rhizomes used over a long period of time can cause irreversible kidney damage, [[haematuria]], and limb paralysis.<ref name=":2" />

== Conservation ==
The plant is categorized as Least Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).<ref name=":2" /> There are currently no conservation tactics in place. However, to maintain the species it is recommended to protect the habitats by reducing human threats like coastal development,  random cutting, overgrazing, local collection practices, tourism, irregular fires, deforestation, and trampling. Although a population decline is seen at some sites such as North Africa ([[Morocco]] and [[Algeria]]), the overall population trend is stable.<ref name=":5" />
